summary: Describes two methods for working out the canonically ordered predecessor and successor of a DNS name. These can be used to synthesize NSEC records on the fly, so servers prove a name does not exist without exposing other names. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: If you want to say there is nothing between two words in a dictionary, you need to find the word just before and just after. This gives ways to find those neighbors.

questions: how to compute dns name neighbors
subtitle: Computing the canonically-ordered predecessor and successor of a DNS name.

tldr.problem: DNSSEC needs to prove that a name does not exist without revealing other names in the zone. This requires computing the predecessor and successor names in canonical order.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes two algorithmic methods: an absolute method that finds exact boundaries, and a modified method that is more efficient but works only with certain zone structures.
tldr.outcome: Servers can now synthesize NSEC records on-the-fly to provide authenticated denial of existence, enabling online signing without exposing all zone contents.

today: RFC 4471 is Experimental. It provides algorithms used by DNSSEC implementations to synthesize NSEC records dynamically, enabling authenticated denial of existence without exposing all zone names.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol is a protocol for querying and modifying directory information over a network. DNSSEC requires a way to answer queries for names that do not exist by proving that no valid name could sit between two known names. This document provides two methods for computing the immediate predecessor and successor of any DNS name in canonical order, which are the boundary names needed for this proof.

The two methods trade off between accuracy and efficiency. The absolute method returns the mathematically exact predecessor and successor, guaranteed to have no valid name between them. The modified method is computationally simpler and produces smaller results but only works for zones with single-label owner names.
sections.plainLanguage: Finding neighbors of a word in a list is easy if you just look at the list. But if you want to prove a word is not there, you need to find the word just before and just after where it would go. The RFC describes how to do this for DNS names.

sections.title: Canonical Order and Notation
sections.content:
DNS names are ordered according to canonical ordering rules defined in RFC 4034. The RFC uses notational conventions to describe the operations: P(N) denotes the immediate predecessor of a name N using the absolute method, S(N) denotes the successor, and P'(N) and S'(N) denote the predecessors and successors using the modified method.

The derivations assume all uppercase US-ASCII letters have been converted to lowercase, since DNS is case-insensitive. The maximum label length is 63 octets and the maximum DNS name length is 255 octets (including the root label). Values are incremented or decremented while skipping octet values that correspond to uppercase ASCII letters, since those should never appear in canonical order.
sections.plainLanguage: There are rules for how to sort DNS names, kind of like alphabetical order but more strict. The document uses a special shorthand to describe the steps, like P(N) meaning 'the name just before N'.

sections.title: The Two Methods
sections.content:
The absolute method handles all cases systematically by padding names to the maximum length and adjusting octets step-by-step. To find the predecessor, it either removes the first label entirely (if it contains all zeros), or decrements the rightmost octet of the first label after padding the label with maximum-value octets. To find the successor, it either prepends a single zero octet in a new label or increments the rightmost non-maximum octet in the first label and discards everything to the right of it.

The modified method is simpler: it works only for zones where owner names have at most one label more than the zone apex. It skips the step of padding to maximum length for predecessors and simplifies the successor computation because it can assume all names fit safely within length limits. This results in smaller, more efficient responses for typical zone structures.
sections.plainLanguage: The absolute way is like checking every single position to make sure you get the exact boundaries. The modified way shortcuts some steps if you promise your zone names are simple enough, making it faster and smaller.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
Several edge cases require attention. Implementing must decide whether to use the full binary range of octets (0x00 to 0xff) or restrict to letter-digit-hyphen values. Using the full range is more general but may create derived names with non-printable octets. Restricting to LDH values produces more readable results and prevents accidental creation of wildcard DNS names (which start with the asterisk octet 0x2a).

Before using a derived predecessor as an NSEC owner name, a server should verify that name actually exists in the zone; if it does, a non-synthesized NSEC record should be used instead. The maximum DNS name length can optionally be restricted to the longest name actually in the zone, which reduces response sizes but reveals information about zone contents.
sections.plainLanguage: When you compute neighbors, you need to decide whether to allow weird characters in the result, and whether to check that the names you compute actually exist or make sense in your zone.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The modified method is somewhat less susceptible to denial-of-service attacks than the absolute method because it tests fewer conditions per derivation, reducing the computational work required per query. Both methods are designed to work in real time without pre-computing all possible predecessors and successors.

The RFC also notes that the derived names may accidentally become wildcards if non-LDH characters are used, or may reveal zone information if the maximum name length is set to the actual longest name in the zone rather than the protocol maximum. Servers should be aware that synthesized NSEC records containing names with unusual octets might confuse faulty resolver implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: Computing neighbors can be done quickly, so an attacker sending lots of queries does not break your server. But you should be careful about weird characters and what information the results reveal about your zone.
